Immunoreactivity scores of patients were calculated according to the following formula: H-score = 100 ⅹ (% cells with score 1 × 1 + % cells with score 2 × 2 + % cells with score 3 × 3), ranging from 0 to 300. For the immunoreactivity assessment of Ki-67 staining, the Ki-67-positive cells were quantified by computerised counts (Image-Pro Plus 6). The TUNEL or 4-HNE positive cells were visually counted by experienced pathologists.

Transmission electron microscopy
Cultured cells and freshly isolated liver tissues were fixed in 0.15 M sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 7.4) supplemented with 2.5% glutaraldehyde, and 2 mM CaCl2 for 2h at 4°C and post-fixed in 1% osmium tetroxide overnight at 4°C and 1% potassium ferricyanide for 12h at room temperature. Then, samples were stained in 1% aqueous uranyl acetate for 1 hour at 4°C in the dark, dehydrated in graded acetones and finally embedded in EMbed 812 (Electron Microscopy Sciences). Ultrathin sections (70 nm) were cut using a diamond knife (Diatome) in an ultramicrotome (Leica EM UC7), placed on copper grids and stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate. Sections were photographed on a JEM 1400 transmission electron microscope operated at 120 kV. Morphometric analysis of maximal cristae width was performed by using Image-pro plus 6 on at least 15 randomly selected mitochondria per group.

Pharmacokinetic studies
A single oral dose of tyrosinol was administered to 8-week-old male Myc/Alb-cre mice. Liver tissues were collected at the indicated time points, extracted with 50% methanol and shaken for 1h before centrifuging at 16,000×g for 10 min at 4°C. LC-MS analysis was performed on the UPLC I-Class chromatography coupled to a XEVO TQ-S Micro triple-quadrupole mass spectrometer with SRM scan type. Target Lynx software was used for the quantitative analysis. Phoenix WinNonlin software (version 8.1) was used to calculate the pharmacokinetic parameters through non-compartmental pharmacokinetic analysis with the linear/log trapezoidal rule.

Oil red O staining assay
HCC cells were seeded in six-well plates, then treated as indicated in the figures. Staining was performed according to the instructions of the Oil Red O Stain Kit (Solarbio, Cat# G1262). Briefly, cells were washed with PBS three times and subsequently fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 min at room temperature. After being rinsed with 60% isopropanol for 10–20s until the stroma was clear, cells were soaked in a newly prepared Oil Red O solution for 20 min before staining with Mayer hematoxylin solution for 1 min. Representative images were recorded using a Nikon fluorescence microscope system, and lipid droplet intensity was assessed with Image-pro plus 6 software.

Cellular fractionation
Cellular fractionation was performed as previously described21. In brief, cells were harvested, and 1/4 of the cells were removed as whole cell lysate (WCL). The remaining cells were lysed in lysis buffer containing 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.9, 10 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.5 mM dithiothreitol and protease inhibitors for 30 min on ice, and then NP-40 (0.3% final concentration) was added to the lysates. The lysates were swirled for 25s and centrifuged at 200×g for 10 min at 4°C to separate the cytoplasmic fraction (Cytoplasm) and the nuclear pellet (Nucleus). The precipitates were resuspended with solution 1 (0.25 M sucrose, 10 mM MgCl2), then added onto solution 2 (0.88 M sucrose, 0.05 mM MgCl2) and centrifuged at 3500×g for 10 min to obtain the purified nuclear fraction.

Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) binding assay
The binding affinity of FjTAL with tyrosine or phenylalanine and YARS1 with tyrosine or tyrosinol was measured using a MicroCal PEAQ-ITC calorimeter. Briefly, all proteins and compounds were dissolved in the working buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 8.0 and 200 mM NaCl). The titration was performed with 19 successive injections of tyrosine or phenylalanine at 300 μM concentration, with a 120s interval between each injection, into the cell solution containing FjTAL at 10 μM concentration at 50×g at 25°C. Correspondingly, tyrosine or tyrosinol with a concentration of 500 μM was titrated into YARS1 at 25 μM concentration. The Origin software was used for baseline correction, integration and isotherm curve fitting to a single-site binding model to calculate the equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) values of binding reactions.

Mitochondrial complex activity
The activities of mitochondrial complex I-V from cells or liver tissues were tested using mitochondrial complex activity assay kit (Solarbio, Cat# BC0515, Cat# BC3235, Cat# BC3245, Cat# BC0945 and Cat# BC1440), respectively, according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Single-cell RNA-seq and analysis
The single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) cohort was obtained from the Cancer Single-cell Expression Map (CancerSCEM) at the China National Centre for Bioinformation (CNCB). Raw data were sourced from the following datasets in the GEO database: GSE107747, GSE202642, GSE242889, GSE233405, and GSE155481. Analysis was conducted using the Seurat v5.2.1 R package. Hepatocyte and hepatocellular carcinoma cell clusters were extracted from CancerSCEM-LIHC (n=10). Cell clusters were defined using the SingleR package, with hepatocellular carcinoma cells and hepatocyte clusters identified based on MYC expression levels. The Dimplot and Featureplot were generated using SCpubr and Nebulosa R packages.

RNA sequencing and data analysis
mRNAs were enriched from total RNA using Oligo dT magnetic beads, followed by fragmentation and synthesis of first and second-strand cDNA. Terminal repair, poly-A addition, adapter ligation, fragment selection, amplification, and purification prepared the library for sequencing on SURFSeq 5000 (GeneMind). Raw reads underwent quality control and filtration before being mapped to the GRCh38/hg38 genome using HISAT2. The feature Counts tools from Subread software filtered non-uniquely mapped and unqualified reads, generating an RNA-seq count matrix. Differential expression gene (DEG) analysis was executed by the DEseq2 (V1.42.1) R packages based on the count matrix. The visualisation of the results of DEGs analysis (Volcano plot) was generated using ggplot2 R package, and the DEGs list was established by setting the log2Foldchange threshold at 1 and p value < 0.05. Data are shown in Supplementary Data 2.

Tandem mass tag-labelled (TMT) quantitative proteomics and analysis
Total proteins were extracted, quantified using BCA assay, digested into peptides and labelled with TMT. These TMT-labelled peptides were fractionated via reversed-phase chromatography on an Agilent 1100 HPLC system and analysed by LC-MS. All analyses were performed by a Q-Exactive mass spectrometer (Thermo, USA) equipped with a Nanospray Flex source (Thermo, USA). Proteome Discoverer (v.2.4) was used to search all the Q-Exactive raw data thoroughly against the sample protein database. Database search was performed with Trypsin digestion specificity. Alkylation of cysteine was considered a fixed modification during database searching. For the protein quantification method, the labelling method was selected. A global false discovery rate (FDR) was set to 0.01, and protein groups considered for quantification required at least two peptides. After peptide quality control and median normalisation, a protein expression level matrix was generated. Inter-group differential protein analysis was conducted using the rstatix (version 0.7.2) R package with a mean-based differential analysis approach. A volcano plot of differential proteins was created using the ggplot2 R package. Data are shown in Supplementary Data 3.

Ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) and data analysis
Cells were collected and washed with ice-cold PBS containing cycloheximide, then snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen. The frozen cell pellets were lysed using ice-cold lysis buffer containing 150 mM Tris-HCl, 10 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.5 mM DTT, 1% NP–40, 100 μg/mL CHX and DNase. The supernatant was treated with RNase, and urea gels were used to isolate ribosome-protected fragments (RPFs). The library was successfully prepared and sequenced using the SURFSeq 5000 platform (GeneMind). The clean reads were obtained by filtering the raw reads, mapped to the GRCh38/hg38 genome, human rRNA sequences, human tRNA sequences, and human CDS or cDNA sequences. Sequencing quality was assessed by RPFs distribution analysis performed using the genomic alignments R package and riboWaltz. Ribo-seq read count matrix was generated using feature counts software by counting the number of reads mapping to the ORF of protein-coding genes. Normalisation and differential translation analysis were performed using the DEseq2 R package. Visualisation of differential translation genes (volcano plot) was generated using the ggplot2 R package. The genome visualisation was performed using the integrative genomics viewer (IGV, version 2.18.4) based on BAM files of each sample mapped to GRCh38/hg38 genome. Data are shown in Supplementary Data 4.

Metabolomics analysis using GC-MS and LC-MS, and data processing
SNU398 cells were seeded in 15-cm plates in tyrosine-restricted medium or normal medium. After 2 days, a total of 1×10⁸ cells were harvested from each group to generate four technical replicates. Then, pre-cooled methanol-water (V:V=4:1) and chloroform were added to the cells, followed by sonication for 20 min in an ice-water bath and standing at −40°C overnight. After being centrifuged at 16,000×g for 10 min at 4°C, 2/3 of the supernatant was removed for LC-MS detection, and the remaining supernatant was used for GC-MS. To perform LC-MS, the dried supernatants were reconstituted with methanol-water (V:V=1:4), and mixed with the internal standard (0.1 mg/mL), vortexed for 30s, sonicated for 3 min in an ice-water bath, and then stood for 2 hours at −40°C. After being centrifuged again at 16,000×g for 10 min at 4°C, the supernatant was aspirated with a syringe, filtered using a 0.22 μm organic-phase pinhole filter, and stored at −80°C for LC-MS analysis. The procedure of GC-MS analysis was described above in amino acid profiling. LC-MS analysis was done by Waters ACQUITY UPLC I-Class plus and Thermo QE system. GC-MS analysis was performed using an Agilent 8890-5977B quadrupole instrument time-of-flight mass spectrometer.

Progenesis QI v3.0 software (Nonlinear Dynamics, Newcastle, UK) was used to pre-process the raw data for baseline filtering, peak identification, integration, retention time correction, peak alignment and normalisation. MS-DIAL software was used to perform qualitative and quantitative analysis of small molecules from GC-MS data collected in Full Scan mode. The identification of compounds was based on multiple dimensions such as RT (retention time), exact mass number, secondary fragments, and isotope distribution. Identification analysis was performed using the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB), Lipidmaps (v2.3), METLIN database, and LuMet Animal 3.0 local database. Data are shown in Supplementary Data 5.

Data mining of genome-wide CRISPR screens
Screen results from the DepMap project (DepMap Public 24Q2+ Score Chronos), visualised through ggplot2 R package were used to identify the dependencies of YARS or tyrosine metabolism-related gene sets in HCC cell lines.

Multi-omics analysis and visualisation
The GSEA analysis based on the KEGG and GO database was performed by clusterProfiler (V4.10.1) R package, and GSEA plot was generated by ggplot2 R package and enrichplot R package. Combination analysis of TCGA with CPTAC, RNA-seq with proteomics, RNA-seq with Ribo-seq, and proteomics with Ribo-seq was performed based on the results of differential analysis of each omics (log2FoldChange) and visualised by ggplot2 R package.

Codon and amino acid frequency analysis
The complete CDS sequences of the human genome were retrieved from the NCBI CCDS database. After filtering all sequences lacking an ATG initiation codon, codon counts for all 64 codon types across CDS sequences were quantified using Biostrings R package. Then, the percentage distribution of each codon within individual CDS sequences was calculated to generate a codon frequency matrix. Subsequently, the amino acid counts and frequency matrix for all 20 amino acids were generated according to the codon table and codon count matrix. Based on the codon and amino acid frequency matrix, we ranked all CDS from high to low based on the frequency of each codon and amino acid, and generated codon TAC and tyrosine frequency distribution curve of all human genome CDS using ggplot2. Next, the differential codons and amino acids of target gene sets screened from multi-omics were calculated based on differential value (log2FoldChange) and codons and amino acids frequency matrix, and the differential codons and amino acids heatmap was generated by ggplot2.

Statistical and reproducibility
All results were shown as the mean ± standard deviation, and the data were from at least three independent experiments unless specifically stated. The statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 10 or the corresponding R packages. GraphPad Prism 10 software was used for mouse survival studies to generate a survival curve and perform statistical significance analysis. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated from RNA sequencing gene expression data and the outcome of 330 hepatocellular carcinomas and analysed for statistical significance using the R software package. An unpaired two-tailed Student’s t test was used to analyse the data for two-group comparisons. ANOVA analysis was used to compare multiple groups as described in the figure legends.

Reporting summary
Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Data availability
The proteomic and metabolome data generated in this study have been deposited in the CNCB database under accession codes OMIX010875 and OMIX010876. The proteomic and metabolomic data are also available under accession code IPX0014937000 in the Integrated Proteome Resources. The RNA-seq and Ribo-seq data generated in this study have been deposited in the CNCB database under accession code HRA012185. The HCC single-cell transcriptome data used in this study are available in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database under accession codes GSE202642, GSE242889, and GSE155481. The raw data of RNA-seq, Ribo-seq, proteomic, and metabolomic data are available under open access. The sequences of primers, shRNA, and probes used in this article are supplied in Supplementary Data 1. The data from transcriptomics, translatomics, proteomics, and metabolomics are supplied in Supplementary Data 2–5, respectively. The raw numbers for charts and graphs are available in the Source Data file. Source data are provided with this paper.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents an extensive mechanistic study on how HCC reprograms tyrosine metabolism to support tumorigenesis by favoring translation over catabolism. The study reveals that MYC driven upregulation of YARS1 and tRNA-Tyr-GUA shunts tyrosine toward protein synthesis, particularly in translation of mitochondrial complex I subunit NDUFB8 and the lipid regulator SCD1. Tyrosine restriction via dietary limitation, enzymatic degradation (TAL), or inhibition of YARS1 (tyrosinol) impairs oxidative phosphorylation and promotes ferroptosis, resulting in reduced tumor burden and increased survival in mouse HCC models. The authors also identify synergistic vulnerabilities via CRISPR screening, highlighting GPX4 and BCL2 inhibition as effective combinatorial strategies. This is a compelling study that uncovers a non-obvious metabolic vulnerability in HCC by targeting translational tyrosine dependency. However, further additional evidence is required to clarify mechanisms and strengthen causal links
Major comments:
1. Given that the central claim is that tyrosine availability fuels tumorigenesis, a direct quantitative comparison (tumor weight, number, size) between 100% and 500% tyrosine diet groups would strengthen this claim. The data presented in fig 1d-f highlight the impact of dietary tyrosine modulation. While the 0% tyrosine diet robustly reduces tumor burden, the reported increase in tumor burden with 500% tyrosine supplementation is mentioned but not fully quantified or statistically interrogated in the main figure panels.
2. Although fig. 2 provides evidence for increased protein incorporation of 3H-tyrosine in HCC and upregulation of YARS1 and tRNA-Tyr-GUA, there is no direct assessment of global protein synthesis under tyrosine-free conditions to determine if tyrosine restriction broadly suppresses translation or specifically affects tyrosine-rich transcripts. An O-propargyl-puromycin (OPP) assay would allow quantification of nascent protein synthesis under tyrosine-free vs. control conditions. This could confirm that global translation remains largely intact and would support the claim that only tyrosine-dependent translation is compromised.
3. The ribosome profiling data in fig. 3 suggest that translation of tyrosine rich transcripts like NDUFB8 and SCD1 is impaired under tyrosine restriction, but the resolution of codon specific stalling (especially at the A or P site) is not reported. Ribosome stalling at tyrosine codons would directly demonstrate codon specific translation stress. Precise mapping of ribosome footprints could reveal whether stalled ribosomes accumulate at Tyr codons in these transcripts, and whether the stalling occurs at the A or P sites, thus validating mechanistic specificity. This reviewer suggests to re-analyze Ribo-seq data with higher resolution A- and P-site mapping around TAC codons in NDUFB8 and SCD1 transcripts. Also, generating cumulative plots showing footprint pileups at Tyr codons under tyrosine-replete vs. tyrosine-deprived conditions in NDUF8 and SCD1 transcripts might be very informative.
4. The luciferase reporters for NDUFB8 and SCD1 translation rely on the native sequence. However, the specificity of RTTA to the TAC codon (vs. TAT) is assumed but not tested. Given that tRNA-Tyr-GUA decodes TAC codons and not TAT, mutating TAC to TAT in the reporter constructs could test codon specificity. If translation inhibition persists with TAT-only reporters, this may suggest off-target or broader effects, whereas rescue would confirm specific targeting of TAC codons via tRNA-Tyr-GUA.
Minor comments:
1.Given the relatively high in vivo dosage of tyrosinol (500 mg/kg), a toxicity and specificity profile is warranted. Are other aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases affected?
2. While ITC data suggest that tyrosinol binds YARS1 with similar affinity as tyrosine, no kinetic data (competitive inhibition or IC50 for aminoacylation) are presented.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript presents a comprehensive study investigating how HCC cells rewire tyrosine metabolism to favour protein translation rather than catabolism, ultimately supporting tumourigenesis. The authors demonstrated that, rather than being catabolized, tyrosine is preferentially diverted toward protein synthesis in HCC. This reprogramming is facilitated through MYC-dependent upregulation of YARS1 and its cognate tRNA, tRNA-TyrGUA. The integration of multi-omics data and functional studies both in vitro and in vivo across human and murine models convincingly show that tyrosine availability is critical for tumour growth and that restricting tyrosine (via diet or enzymatically) or inhibiting YARS1 impairs tumour progression. The authors provide a compelling rationale for targeting tyrosine utilization as a therapeutic approach in liver cancer. This study will be of broad interest to readers of Nature Communications, particularly those interested in cancer metabolism and translational oncology. While the conclusions are largely supported by the data, several conceptual and mechanistic aspects would benefit from clarification or additional experimentation. For example, the role of the integrated stress response (ISR), which is notably absent from the discussion despite its relevance in amino acid sensing.
Specific comments:
1. Figure 1D-F : Systemic effects of tyrosine-deficient diets. It is unclear whether the systemic consequences of tyrosine-deficient diets were controlled for. Were there differences in food intake, body weight (lean mass/fat mass), or signs of hepatic dysfunction. Given that tyrosine is also an important precursor to several neurotransmitters, including data from healthy, wild-type animals subjected to these diets would be beneficial and bolster any translational relevance.
2. Are tyrosine-restricted diets administered prior to tumour initiation, or after tumours are established? It would be important to evaluate whether dietary intervention would still be effective when tumours are already present or larger.
3. Since phenylalanine is a precursor to tyrosine, how do the authors explain the apparent complete depletion of Tyr under ‘0% tyrosine’ conditions in vitro ( is there no tyrosine biosynthesis or is this insufficient to meet the demands of the cells)? Stable isotope tracing experiments with phenylalanine may help explain this.
4. Figure 1I-J: please include isotopologue abundances in addition to fractional enrichment in the 13C-Tyr tracing data.
5. Are the observed Tyr dependencies a general feature of liver tumourigenesis, or specifically driven by MYC dysregulation? Authors mention that 11.56% of HCC patients observe MYC amplification, but the cell lines used (SNU398, SNU449, and Huh7) do not have MYC amplification. Correlating Tyr sensitivity with MYC expression would address this- does MYC KD reduce tyrosine dependency or rescue effects of tyrosine depletion?
6. Figure 2O-2Q show that some HCC cell lines are highly dependent on YARS1. Do these correspond to MYC-high models? Does YARS1 correlate with MYC expression levels or general translation rates?
7. Is the reduction in tyrosine metabolic genes in HCC cells and tumours MYC-dependent?
8. If YARS1 is knocked down, can the observed mitochondrial and lipid peroxidation defects be rescued by re-expressing SCD1 or NDUFB8?
9. ISR Pathway : the authors make no mention to the ISR which is canonically activated in response to AA limitation via GCN2/eif2a/ATF4. This is a key mechanistic gap, especially since uncharged tRNAs are canonical activators of GCN2, several markers observed (e.g. SLC7A5, SLC7A11, oxidative stress response genes) are known ATF4 target genes, and proteins upregulated upon tyrosine deprivation are clustered in hallmarks that are common to amino acid restriction (autophagy, L-amino acid transport etc). The ISR could influence lipid metabolism and ferroptosis, potentially confounding the attribution to SCD1 downregulation. Have the authors assessed ISR activation in response to tyrosine depletion or YARS1 KD? This pathway should be acknowledged.
10. Fatty acid metabolism and link to ferroptosis: fatty acid composition is known to change under metabolic stress or ISR activation. Can the authors uncouple the effects of tyrosine depletion on MUFA/PUFA balance from its protenogenic role in SCD1 synthesis? Would MUFA supplementation rescue ferroptosis induced by tyrosine depletion, MYC KD, or YARS1 KD? Does SCD1 KD alone recapitulate the lipid peroxidation phenotypes?
11. Figure S1L/S1N and S1A/S1C: Does the proliferation increase with tyrosine supplementation correlate with increased protein expression of SCD1 and NDUFB8?
12. Figure 1I: the 12-hour labelling time is relatively long to assess amino acid uptake. The increase in M+6 Tyr could be due to decreased catabolism rather than increased uptake. Use of transporter inhibition (eg. JPH203 for SLC7A5) or transporter KD would clarify this mechanism.
13. Figure 1C: tumour size negatively correlates with Tyr concentration. Can authors measure tyrosine levels in tumour interstitial fluid to confirm that this doesn’t reflect local tyrosine availability?
14. Line 70-71: The statement that “low levels of tyr favour liver tumourigenesis” seems contradictory given that later data show increased tyrosine uptake and that tyrosine supplementation boosts HCC proliferation. Should reframe to clarify that tumours have an increased requirement for tyrosine.
15. Figure 2B/2C , Lines 126-128: The enrichment of tyrosine codons in translationally upregulated proteins may reflect general increases in protein synthesis. Would this not also be true for other amino acids? Is this increased utilization of tyrosine for protein synthesis tyrosine-specific or a global phenomenon associated with tumour progression?
16. In Figure 3 the effect of the tyrosine-deficient diet on specific proteins is evaluated in tumour cell lines and is also shown for tumours. Are those effects tumour-specific, i.e. are the levels of SCD1 and NDUF8 affected by Tyr-deficient diet in the adjacent liver tissue of tumour-bearing mice? They do have tissues so would be important to see of NDUF8 and SCD1 are also affected in normal livers.
17. Would the expression of NDUF8 and SCD1 proteins also be affected if any other amino acids are depleted?
18. The increase in PUFA levels upon tyrosine deprivation is surprising. Do authors have a plausible explanation?
19. Were tyrosine levels measured with FjTAL treatment?
General comment: a lot of panels should be moved to supplemental or additional information to make main figures less crowded and the main points more concise.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This study explores hepatocellular carcinoma's metabolic plasticity, focusing on how HCC cells reprogram tyrosine uptake and use to promote translation rather than catabolism. It presents extensive data integrating metabolomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, ribosome profiling, CRISPR screening, and in vivo models. The idea that tyrosine translation availability (RTTA) is a vulnerability in HCC and can be targeted is potentialy clinically relevant. The concepts appear to be novel, however, despite the comprehensive data, several weaknesses diminish the mechanistic insights and translational impact.
Major Concerns
1. The genome-wide CRISPR screen is used as a central aspect to identify synthetic vulnerabilities in the RTTA context. However, the changes observed are modest, and the study subsequently relies largely on pharmacological inhibitors (e.g., venetoclax, RSL3, erastin, sorafenib) to support claims. The reliance on small-molecule inhibitors with pleiotropic effects makes it difficult to attribute synergy specifically to RTTA-related pathways. As such, validation using genetic loss-of-functon(knockout/knockdown) models for key hits (e.g., GPX4, SLC7A11, BCL2) is essential. Rescue experiments with ferroptosis inhibitors (e.g., ferrostatin-1, β-mercaptoethanol) would help confirm the ferroptotic mechanism.
2. Sorafenib is a multi-kinase inhibitor with broad targets beyond ferroptosis. Venetoclax also has complex effects on apoptosis. Without genetic proof, the observed synergy between tyrosine restriction and these agents may reflect unrelated drug effects rather than specific mechanistic interactions with RTTA. For this, it would be relevant to include in vivo experiments with genetically defined ferroptosis-sensitive models, such as Xct (SLC7A11) or GPX4 deficient cells (important to note that these cells cannot growth in vitro without β-mercaptoethanol or ferrostatin-1 respectively – but in the presence of these agent knockout cells can be generate and implanted in vivo). These experiments would provide strong mechanistic validation that RTTA acts via ferroptosis.
3. The study convincingly shows reduced tyrosine metabolism and increased translation, but the direct causality between MYC → YARS1 → translation of ETC components and ferroptosis is not fully established. Would experiments using codon-recoding of NDUFB8/SCD1 reduce tyrosine dependence? This experiments while challenging could strengthen the link between codon usage bias and ferroptotic outcomes.
Minor Concerns
• The dietary intervention (TR diet) is intriguing, but patient feasibility is uncertain. A discussion of nutritional safety, systemic effects, and whether restriction selectively affects tumor cells versus normal hepatocytes is necessary.
• Tyrosinol and TAL enzyme approaches are promising, but off-target metabolic effects remain underexplored. More profiling of systemic amino acid metabolism would be important before translational claims.
• Figures: Several panels are highly data-dense. Consider streamlining or moving supportive proteomic/transcriptomic heatmaps to Supplementary Figures.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
The manuscript titled “Targeting tRNA-dependent tyrosine usage unveils a metabolic vulnerability in hepatocellular carcinoma” described tyrosine charging to tRNA and its subsequent utilization for protein translation as a metabolic dependency for the tumorigenesis of HCC and demonstrated that limiting the availability of tyrosine for translation attenuates tumorigenesis. Specifically, the authors reported that free tyrosine levels are significantly reduced in human and mouse HCC tumors compared to normal tissues and that this reduction in tyrosine levels is attributed to MYC-dependent increased tyrosine charging to form tRNA-TyrGUA, which is needed for protein translation.
To demonstrate the dependence of HCC on the availability of tyrosine charging and its subsequent translation, the authors showed that limiting tyrosine translation availability—via dietary limitation, YARS1/tRNA-TyrGUA ablation, tyrosine degradation (TAL), or YARS1 inhibition (tyrosinol)—leads to impaired oxidative phosphorylation and ferroptosis and attenuation of tumor progression in several mouse models. Mechanistically, the authors showed that restriction of tyrosine translation availability reduces tyrosine codon-dependent translation of mitochondrial complex I subunit NDUFB8 and lipid regulator SCD1, causing complex I misassembly, oxidative phosphorylation failure, and lipid peroxidation-induced ferroptosis.
Based on these findings, the authors concluded that tRNA-dependent tyrosine usage is a metabolic vulnerability of HCC that can be exploited for therapeutic treatment. While there are some issues with the interpretation of the data and some claims made are not well-founded, the authors have compilled relevant data to support their claims, and the discovery of the role of tRNA-dependent tyrosine usage in HCC is rather novel and potentially important. If the authors could address some of the flaws in the current version of the manuscript, the manuscript should be at the level of Nature Communications.
Major Flaws and Issues:
1. One of the problems reading through the manuscript and figures is that the authors crammed too many data points into each figure. For example, to describe the effects of various treatments on tumor growth, the authors used non-liver body weight (body weight minus liver weight) to show that treatments did not have an impact on non-liver body weight. These data are probably not necessary to include in the main figures. I would suggest the authors move less relevant figures to the supplement to avoid overwhelming the figures and readers (this makes some figures barely eligible such as Figures 1C, 3E, 3I, 3K, and 3L).
2. One of the major claims in the manuscript is that restricting tRNA-dependent tyrosine usage attenuates HCC tumorigenesis and progression by reducing codon-dependent translation of mitochondrial complex I subunit NDUFB8 and lipid regulator SCD1. This would imply that disrupting the expression and/or activity of NDUFB8 and SCD1 could similarly affect HCC tumorigenesis and progression as restricting tRNA-dependent tyrosine usage. Could the authors provide data to test this hypothesis?
3. As a follow-up, what makes the translation of NDUFB8 and SCD1 more susceptible to tyrosine restriction? Given that tyrosine is an amino acid required for synthesizing all tyrosine-containing proteins, it is reasonable to assume that proteins with high tyrosine content in their sequences would be more likely to be affected by tyrosine restriction. Could the authors survey protein databases to identify proteins with a high percentage of tyrosine and determine whether NDUFB8 and SCD1 are among them? That piece of data would strengthen the argument made in the manuscript.
4. The authors created three HCC mouse models to demonstrate the efficacy of tyrosine restriction (Figures 1D–F). However, in the figure legends, the authors did not provide a clear indication of which mouse model was used in subsequent figures (e.g., Figures 1M, 2E), making it hard to interpret the data. Please specify the mouse models used in the figure legends.
5. In Figure 2, the authors claimed that the upregulation of YARS is driven by MYC overexpression. Given that MYC is only responsible for driving a fraction of HCC tumors, it is assumed that this observation is likely specific to MYC-dependent HCC. Is YARS also upregulated in DEN-induced HCC mouse models?
6. In Figure 3, the authors stated that restriction of tyrosine translation availability leads to impaired oxidative stress and ferroptosis. However, the data provided in Figure 3 showed that, while limiting tyrosine upregulates several ferroptosis suppressors such as GPX4 and SLC7A11, it did not directly induce ferroptosis, as the authors have not tested whether ferroptosis inhibitors could rescue the cell death or measured whether tyrosine limitation induces lipid peroxidation. The data provided can only support a claim that tyrosine limitation increases ferroptosis sensitivity rather than leading to ferroptosis. Therefore, the authors need to tone down their claims that limiting tyrosine leads to ferroptosis.
7. In Figure 4, the authors showed that a genome-wide CRISPR screen under tyrosine restriction identified a list of genes, including anti-apoptotic protein BCL2 and anti-ferroptosis proteins SLC7A11 and GPX4, which synergize with tyrosine restriction to promote cell death upon knockout. The authors further validated that pharmacological inhibition of BCL2 or ferroptosis induction using SLC7A11 inhibitors or GPX4 inhibitors could synergize with dietary tyrosine limitation and YARS1 depletion to promote HCC cell death in vitro and attenuate HCC tumor growth in vivo. These data are largely consistent with those provided in Figure 3, showing that tyrosine restriction promotes ferroptosis sensitivity. However, Figure 3 is titled as “Restriction of tyrosine translation availability leads to impaired oxidative stress and ferroptosis” and was allocated to show that tyrosine restriction promotes ferroptosis sensitivity. Thus, it would make more sense to rearrange and consolidate these ferroptosis-related data into one figure. It would take some effort to rearrange and adjust the text accordingly, but it would significantly improve the manuscript’s logical flow.
8. In Figures 4, 5, and 6, the authors showed some representative images of liver tumors (4I, 4L, 5N, and 6N) after treatment. Some of these liver tumors appeared completely tumor-free, yet the survival of the mice from these treatment groups (4K, 4N, 5P, and 6P) was extended but not completely protected. While this may sound like nitpicking and fastidious criticism, it does make readers question how representative these tumor images are. I would recommend selecting more representative and realistic images to avoid being nitpicked.
9. The authors used TEM images of livers to show that cristae formation was severely affected by tyrosine limitation via dietary limitation, YARS1/tRNA-TyrGUA ablation, tyrosine degradation (TAL), or YARS1 inhibition (tyrosinol) and quantified maximal cristae width to show that these treatments lead to mitochondrial defects. While these images are on the same scale based on the scale bar, the mitochondrial size and electron density vary significantly. For example, in Figure 6S, the tyrosinol group showed clearly smaller and more electron-dense mitochondria compared to the control-treated ones. These images are not quite comparable in scale, making it difficult to quantify maximal cristae width. I would recommend selecting more comparable images as representative images.
10. In several figures (Figures 5K–L, 6J–K), the authors showed that in HCC cell lines, tyrosine degradation (TAL) or YARS1 inhibition (tyrosinol) increases lipid peroxidation, suggesting that these treatments induce ferroptosis. It would be more convincing if the authors could also test whether ferrostatin or an iron chelator could attenuate the lipid oxidation induced by these treatments.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewers’ comments
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author); expert in translation regulation:
This manuscript presents an extensive mechanistic study on how HCC reprograms tyrosine metabolism to support tumorigenesis by favoring translation over catabolism.
The study reveals that MYC driven upregulation of YARS1 and tRNA-Tyr-GUA shunts tyrosine toward protein synthesis, particularly in translation of mitochondrial complex I subunit NDUFB8 and the lipid regulator SCD1. Tyrosine restriction via dietary limitation, enzymatic degradation (TAL), or inhibition of YARS1 (tyrosinol) impairs oxidative phosphorylation and promotes ferroptosis, resulting in reduced tumor burden and increased survival in mouse HCC models. The authors also identify synergistic vulnerabilities via CRISPR screening, highlighting GPX4 and BCL2 inhibition as effective combinatorial strategies.
This is a compelling study that uncovers a non-obvious metabolic vulnerability in HCC by targeting translational tyrosine dependency. However, further additional evidence is required to clarify mechanisms and strengthen causal links.
Response: We appreciate the constructive comments from the reviewer, which will help us further strengthen our manuscript. We have carefully revised the manuscript according to the Reviewer’s comments and provided point-by-point responses as follows.
Major comments:
1. Given that the central claim is that tyrosine availability fuels tumorigenesis, a direct quantitative comparison (tumor weight, number, size) between 100% and 500% tyrosine diet groups would strengthen this claim. The data presented in fig 1d-f highlight the impact of dietary tyrosine modulation. While the 0% tyrosine diet robustly reduces tumor burden, the reported increase in tumor burden with 500% tyrosine supplementation is mentioned but not fully quantified or statistically interrogated in the main figure panels.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments. The quantitative comparisons (including tumor weight, number, and size) between the 100% and 500% tyrosine diet groups are presented in Figures S1B-S1D of the revised manuscript, due to space limitations (please also see Response Figure 1-1). In the three models (MYC overexpression-driven HCC model, DEN treatment-induced HCC model, and intrahepatic injection model of human HCC cells), dietary tyrosine supplementation (Tyr 500% diet) led to a significant increase in characteristic hepatomegaly, liver-to-body weight ratio, tumor burdens, and diameters relative to the standard diet (Tyr 100% diet), indicating that tyrosine supplementation promotes liver cancer development. The related description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 4, Lines 83-84).
Response Figure 1-1. (A) A diagram depicting the in vivo assessment of tumorigenesis by tyrosine in Myc/Alb-cre mice (top), C57BL/6J mice treated by DEN (middle), and BALB/c nude mice with HCCLM3 cells intrahepatic injection (bottom). (B) Photographs of the liver from the tumor-bearing mice fed either a normal diet (Tyr 100%) or a tyrosine-supplemental diet (Tyr 500%), including Myc/Alb-cre mice (top), C57BL/6J mice (middle), and BALB/c nude mice (bottom). (C) The body weight excluding liver weight, liver to body weight ratio, tumor number, and maximum tumor diameter of the tumor-bearing mice fed tyrosine-modified diet were shown, including Myc/Alb-cre mice (top) (n = 7), C57BL/6J mice (middle) (n = 7), and BALB/c nude mice (bottom) (n = 5).
2. Although fig. 2 provides evidence for increased protein incorporation of 3H-tyrosine in HCC and upregulation of YARS1 and tRNA-Tyr-GUA, there is no direct assessment of global protein synthesis under tyrosine-free conditions to determine if tyrosine restriction broadly suppresses translation or specifically affects tyrosine-rich transcripts. An O-propargyl-puromycin (OPP) assay would allow quantification of nascent protein synthesis under tyrosine-free vs. control conditions. This could confirm that global translation remains largely intact and would support the claim that only tyrosine-dependent translation is compromised.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this great question. To evaluate whether tyrosine restriction broadly suppresses translation, we first analyzed our ribosome-profiling data. As shown in Response Figure 1-2 A (corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S10H), the empirical cumulative distribution of translation efficiency for 5188 genes in SNU398 cells cultured in control media revealed a weak shift in the curve relative to tyrosine-restricted media, indicating that global translation efficiency remained unchanged under tyrosine restriction. Next, the O-propargyl-puromycin (OPP) assay also showed that restricting tyrosine translation availability via tyrosine-free or YARS1 knockdown did not change nascent protein synthesis (Response Figure 1-2 B and C, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S10I and S10J). These results consistently indicate that global translation remains largely intact under tyrosine restriction conditions. The related description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 11, Lines 273-275).
Response Figure 1-2. (A) The empirical cumulative distribution of translation efficiency for 5188 genes in SNU398 cells cultured in control and tyrosine-restricted media. (B and C) Representative images of in vitro OPP incorporation show unchanged nascent protein synthesis in the indicated cells. DAPI, 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole.
3. The ribosome profiling data in fig. 3 suggest that translation of tyrosine rich transcripts like NDUFB8 and SCD1 is impaired under tyrosine restriction, but the resolution of codon specific stalling (especially at the A or P site) is not reported. Ribosome stalling at tyrosine codons would directly demonstrate codon specific translation stress. Precise mapping of ribosome footprints could reveal whether stalled ribosomes accumulate at Tyr codons in these transcripts, and whether the stalling occurs at the A or P sites, thus validating mechanistic specificity. This reviewer suggests to re-analyze Ribo-seq data with higher resolution A- and P-site mapping around TAC codons in NDUFB8 and SCD1 transcripts. Also, generating cumulative plots showing footprint pileups at Tyr codons under tyrosine-replete vs. tyrosine-deprived conditions in NDUF8 and SCD1 transcripts might be very informative.
Response: Thanks for your professional advice. To obtain higher precision RPF sequence alignment information, we strictly restricted the read length range (25-34nt) during sequence filtering and realigned the RPFs to the genome with base-pair precision using STAR. After precisely locating the P-sites and A-sites of all RPFs mapping to the CDS sequences (SCD transcript: ENST00000370355 and NDUFB8 transcript: ENST00000299166), we calculated the relative positions of all these ribosomal footprints represented by RPFs with respect to the nearest TAC codons on the transcripts, and plotted ribosomal footprint accumulation around TAC codons. Additionally, we analyzed the frequency of RPFs exhibiting P-site stalling and A-site stalling at TAC codons in both transcripts.
Based on the reanalysis results of Ribo-seq raw data, tyrosine restriction resulted in a higher frequency of ribosomal footprints at the TAC codon relative to normal conditions, with predominant A-site stalling observed rather than P-site stalling (Response Figure 1-3 A and B, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S10K. The data in the figure sourcing from the Response Table 1 and 2). Footprint accumulation density analysis further revealed that in the SCD1 transcript, the tyrosine-restricted group showed a higher frequency of ribosomal footprints with P-site accumulation at the codon immediately preceding the 5’ end of the TAC codon, confirming that tyrosine deprivation leads to A-site stalling of ribosomes at TAC codons (Response Figure 1-3 C, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S10L). No significant difference in footprint accumulation density was observed in the NDUFB8 transcript, potentially due to an insufficient number of RPFs aligned to this transcript (Response Figure 1-3 D, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S10L). The related description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 12, Lines 293-302).
Response Figure 1-3. (A and B) The frequency of ribosome footprint stalling at TAC codon and the A-site and P-site stalling frequency at TAC codon in the SCD1 and NDUFB8 transcripts. (C and D) The accumulation plot of ribosome footprint around TAC codon ±12nt in the SCD1 (C) and NDUFB8(D) transcripts.

4. The luciferase reporters for NDUFB8 and SCD1 translation rely on the native sequence. However, the specificity of RTTA to the TAC codon (vs. TAT) is assumed but not tested. Given that tRNA-Tyr-GUA decodes TAC codons and not TAT, mutating TAC to TAT in the reporter constructs could test codon specificity. If translation inhibition persists with TAT-only reporters, this may suggest off-target or broader effects, whereas rescue would confirm specific targeting of TAC codons via tRNA-Tyr-GUA.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful point. As the reviewer suggested, we mutated TAC to TAT in the reporter constructs, as shown in the schematic diagram (Response Figure 1-4 A, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S13C). The Relative luciferase activity was higher in SNU398 cells transfected with the MUT reporter constructs (for NDUFB8 or SCD1) than in those with the WT constructs, under tyrosine-free conditions or upon YARS1 knockdown (Response Figure 1-4 B and C, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S13D and S13E), indicating that restricting tyrosine translation availability has a greater translation inhibition effect on TAC-rich transcripts than TAT-rich transcripts. The related description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 14, Lines 355-359).
Response Figure 1-4. (A) Graphic illustration of the indicated reporter expressing luciferase infusion with either SCD1 or NDUFB8 with a different TAC codon frequency. RLuc serves as an internal control. (B and C) Relative luciferase activities in SNU398 cells transfected with the indicated reporters and cultured in tyrosine-modified mediums (B) or relative luciferase activities in SNU398 cells transfected with the indicated reporters together with YARS1 shRNA (C). Quantification of luciferase activities normalized to Renilla luciferase activities (n = 3).
Minor comments:
1. Given the relatively high in vivo dosage of tyrosinol (500 mg/kg), a toxicity and specificity profile is warranted. Are other aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases affected?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments. To evaluate the safety profile of tyrosinol in mice, we first analyzed organ weights upon tyrosinol treatment and found that tyrosinol treatment (repeated dosing of 500 mg/kg/d for 4 weeks, oral gavage) did not result in any significant changes (Response Figure 1-5 A, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S24E). Concurrently, the levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), creatinine, creatine kinase, and lactate dehydrogenase, established biomarkers for liver, kidney, and myocardial injury, were measured. Tyrosinol treatment showed no significant effects on these markers (Response Figure 1-5 B, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S24F). Furthermore, no apparent pathological differences or tissue injury were observed after tyrosinol treatment (500 mg/kg/d) (Response Figure 1-5 C, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S24G). These results indicate that tyrosinol treatment did not induce tissue injury, consistent with a previous study demonstrating that dietary tyrosinol supplementation (10 g/kg in the chow) caused no differences in physiological indices (Figure S7E-S7H) (Zhao et al, 2023) (PMID: 37071536). The related description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 22, Lines 603-608). Additionally, we examined the impact on the aminoacylation of the other two aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine and tryptophan) after tyrosinol treatment. Results demonstrated that the charged tRNA-PheGAA and tRNA-TrpCCA levels remained unchanged upon tyrosinol treatment, indicating that tyrosinol treatment does not have potential off-target effects in vivo (Response Figure 1-5 D, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S24H). The related description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 22, Lines 608-613).
Response Figure 1-5. (A) Male C57BL/6J mice were treated with vehicle or Tyrosinol. The weight of body, liver, kidney, heart, lung and colon were measured. (B) Serum levels of ALT, AST, CREA, CK and LDH were determined in mice treated with vehicle or tyrosinol. (C) H&E staining of liver, kidney, heart, lung and colon from mice treated with vehicle or tyrosinol. Scale bar 100 µm. (n=5).
2. While ITC data suggest that tyrosinol binds YARS1 with similar affinity as tyrosine, no kinetic data (competitive inhibition or IC50 for aminoacylation) are presented.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer's helpful comments. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (AARSs) produce aminoacylated tRNAs for protein synthesis. As shown in Response Figure 1-6 A, the amino acid is first activated by ATP (blue box). Activated amino acid is then transferred to the tRNA (green box). The full aminoacylation pathway (purple box) is marked by the dissociation of the aminoacyl-tRNA from the enzyme. Thus, the aminoacylation rate can be measured by the formation of PPi. Based on this, the production of PPi is measured via a fluorogenic PPi sensor according to the manual of the PhosphoWorksFluorimetric Pyrophosphate Assay Kit *Enhanced Selectivity* (AAT Bioquest, Cat#21614) (Zong et al, 2024) (PMID: 38653238). The results demonstrated that tyrosinol could reduce the binding capacity of YARS1 to tyrosine, as evidenced by IC50 and the increased K (Response Figure 1-6 B, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S22A). The relevant description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 21, Lines 581-583). The detailed description of the pyrophosphate production assay has also been added to the revised manuscript (Page 37, Lines 986-991).
Response Figure 1-6. (A) Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase aminoacylation pathway. (B) The PPi production assay validates the competitive inhibition of tyrosinol on tyrosine binding to YARS1, as evidenced by the increased K in B (left). The PPi production is measured at a tyrosine concentration of 50 μM under treatment with varying concentrations of tyrosinol to calculate its half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) (right). Data are representative of three independent experiments (n = 3).
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author); expert in liver cancer and metabolism:
This manuscript presents a comprehensive study investigating how HCC cells rewire tyrosine metabolism to favour protein translation rather than catabolism, ultimately supporting tumourigenesis. The authors demonstrated that, rather than being catabolized, tyrosine is preferentially diverted toward protein synthesis in HCC. This reprogramming is facilitated through MYC-dependent upregulation of YARS1 and its cognate tRNA, tRNA-TyrGUA. The integration of multi-omics data and functional studies both in vitro and in vivo across human and murine models convincingly show that tyrosine availability is critical for tumour growth and that restricting tyrosine (via diet or enzymatically) or inhibiting YARS1 impairs tumour progression. The authors provide a compelling rationale for targeting tyrosine utilization as a therapeutic approach in liver cancer. This study will be of broad interest to readers of Nature Communications, particularly those interested in cancer metabolism and translational oncology. While the conclusions are largely supported by the data, several conceptual and mechanistic aspects would benefit from clarification or additional experimentation. For example, the role of the integrated stress response (ISR), which is notably absent from the discussion despite its relevance in amino acid sensing.
Response: We would like to express our sincere appreciation to you for taking the time to read the manuscript in-depth and for providing valuable constructive suggestions that will help improve our paper. We learned a great deal from the comments and made our best efforts to revise the manuscript accordingly.
Specific comments:
1. Figure 1D-F : Systemic effects of tyrosine-deficient diets. It is unclear whether the systemic consequences of tyrosine-deficient diets were controlled for. Were there differences in food intake, body weight (lean mass/fat mass), or signs of hepatic dysfunction. Given that tyrosine is also an important precursor to several neurotransmitters, including data from healthy, wild-type animals subjected to these diets would be beneficial and bolster any translational relevance.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical point regarding the systemic effects of tyrosine deprivation. In response to this question, we conducted a dedicated study in healthy, wild-type mice fed a diet deficient in tyrosine. Our results indicate that the 10-week tyrosine-deficient diets induce an increase in total body weight and fat mass, along with increased liver weight (Response Figure 2-1 A and B, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S3A and S3B). No significant differences were observed in the weight of other organs or in daily food intake (Response Figure 2-1 B and C, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S3B and S3C). Concurrently, the levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), triglyceride (TG), total cholesterol (TC), creatinine (CREA), creatine kinase (CK), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), established biomarkers for liver, kidney, and myocardial injury, were measured. Tyrosine-deficient diets increase serum ALT, TC, and TG levels, accompanied by lipid droplet accumulation (Response Figure 2-1 D and E, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S3D and S3E), partially consistent with a previous report (Sano et al, 2021) (PMID: 33724516). This report showed that combined dietary deprivation of tyrosine and methionine reduced the intermediate metabolite fumarate, thereby reducing KEAP1 succinylation and suppressing nuclear translocation of NRF2, ultimately disrupting lipid metabolism and exacerbating hepatic steatosis in high-fat diet-induced non-alcoholic fatty liver disease model (Sano et al., 2021) (PMID: 33724516). Furthermore, in our new experiments, no pathological changes or tissue injury were observed in other organs (Response Figure 2-1 D and E, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S3D and S3E). We did not observe significant differences between the two diet groups during the short-term intervention period in WT mice (2-week or 4-week feeding). The related description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 5, Line 102 to Page 6, Line 115).
Moreover, given tyrosine’s role as a dopamine precursor, we evaluated depression-like behaviors using the tail suspension test (TST), a method for assessing depressive states in mice. No significant behavioral differences were observed between the two diet groups after 10 weeks of intervention (Response Figure 2-1 F, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S3F). It was noted that an 8-month tyrosine-deficient diet in our original DEN-induced HCC model resulted in some hair appearing grayish white, due to tyrosine acting as a precursor for melanin (Data not shown). However, short-term dietary restriction did not alter hair color. Notably, another study finds that tyrosine restriction extends lifespan in Drosophila by activating FOXO pathway, demonstrating the multifaceted effects of tyrosine-restricted diets on physiological processes in a context-dependent manner (Kosakamoto et al, 2024) (PMID: 39213345).
Therefore, for tyrosine restriction diets, it might be safe to apply them intermittently for HCC treatment. Clinical application of tyrosine restriction diets also requires optimization of the intervention time to leverage potential anti-tumor effects while minimizing adverse outcomes. The related description (Page 6, Lines 115-121) and discussion (Page 25, Lines 663-680) have been added to the revised manuscript.
Response Figure 2-1. (A and B) Male C57BL/6J mice were fed either a standard diet or a tyrosine-restricted diet for 10 weeks. The weights of the body, lean mass, fat mass, liver, kidney, heart, lung, and colon were measured. (C) The food intake was counted in C57BL/6J mice fed either a standard diet or a tyrosine-restricted diet for 10 weeks. (D) Serum levels of ALT, AST, TG, TC, CREA, CK, and LDH were determined in the indicated mice. (E) H&E staining of liver, kidney, heart, lung, and colon from the indicated mice. Scale bar 100 µm. (F) The tail suspension test was performed on the indicated mice. (n=5).
2. Are tyrosine-restricted diets administered prior to tumour initiation, or after tumours are established? It would be important to evaluate whether dietary intervention would still be effective when tumours are already present or larger.
Response: We appreciate this thoughtful comment. In our study, we used hepatocyte-specific MYC overexpressing mice, a model that reliably induces early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) lesions (2–3 mm in diameter) by 7 weeks of age in male mice, with progression to advanced-stage tumors (>1 cm) by approximately 3 months (Mei et al, 2020) (PMID: 32489910). In the original manuscript, a tyrosine-restricted diet is introduced at 6 weeks of age, prior to the tumor initiation. In the revised manuscript, at 9 weeks of age, after tumors have already developed, tyrosine-restricted diets were applied to evaluate their impact on established tumorigenesis. Results also indicated that restriction of dietary tyrosine intake (Tyr 0% diet) led to a significant decrease in characteristic hepatomegaly, liver-to-body weight ratio, tumor burdens, and diameters relative to the standard diet (Tyr 100% diet) (Response Figure 2-2, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S1E-1G). These findings indicate that tyrosine-restricted diets exert significant therapeutic efficacy against HCC development during tumor initiation and establishment. The related description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 5, Lines 87-93).
Response Figure 2-2. (A) A diagram depicting the in vivo assessment of tumorigenesis by tyrosine in Myc/Alb-cre mice. (B) Photographs of the liver from the tumor-bearing mice fed either a normal diet or a tyrosine-supplemental diet in Myc/Alb-cre mice. (C) The body weight excluding liver weight, liver to body weight ratio, tumor number, and maximum tumor diameter of the tumor-bearing mice fed a tyrosine-modified diet were shown in Myc/Alb-cre mice (n = 6).
3. Since phenylalanine is a precursor to tyrosine, how do the authors explain the apparent complete depletion of Tyr under ‘0% tyrosine’ conditions in vitro ( is there no tyrosine biosynthesis or is this insufficient to meet the demands of the cells)? Stable isotope tracing experiments with phenylalanine may help explain this.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this great question. We apologize that the y-axis range in Figure S6K of the original manuscript may lead to misinterpretation of the data. We redraw the figure to better represent the differences, as shown in Response Figure 2-3A (corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S11F). Based on our metabolomics results, we observed that under ‘0% tyrosine’ conditions in vitro, intracellular tyrosine levels decreased dramatically, but were still maintained at 17499 of tyrosine abundance, possibly due to phenylalanine as a precursor to tyrosine (Response Figure 2-3 A).
As noted by the reviewer, phenylalanine serves as a precursor to tyrosine and can be converted to tyrosine within the cell. Analysis of our metabolomics data revealed that phenylalanine levels also decreased significantly by approximately 40% after tyrosine restriction, suggesting a rise in phenylalanine consumption (average phenylalanine abundance: Tyr 100% vs Tyr 0% = 434396 vs 255198) (Response Figure 2-3 B). These results collectively indicate that cellular capacity to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine is enhanced following tyrosine restriction. However, this increased conversion might still be insufficient to compensate for the consumption of tyrosine, ultimately leading to a significant decrease in intracellular tyrosine levels. 5. Are the observed Tyr dependencies a general feature of liver tumourigenesis, or specifically driven by MYC dysregulation? Authors mention that 11.56% of HCC patients observe MYC amplification, but the cell lines used (SNU398, SNU449, and Huh7) do not have MYC amplification. Correlating Tyr sensitivity with MYC expression would address this- does MYC KD reduce tyrosine dependency or rescue effects of tyrosine depletion?
Response: We appreciate this thoughtful comment. In our original manuscript, we utilized three distinct mouse HCC models: a MYC overexpression-driven HCC model, a DEN treatment-induced HCC model, and an intrahepatic injection model of human HCC cells, to validate the effect of tyrosine levels on HCC development. Based on our findings (revised manuscript Figure 1), we observed that in all three models, restricting dietary tyrosine intake significantly reduced the development of liver tumors compared to the standard diet, regardless of whether it was associated with MYC amplification. The occurrence of liver cancer induced by DEN is attributed to the formation of methylated macromolecules induced-DNA damage (Schulien & Hasselblatt, 2021) (PMID: 33785162). Moreover, in the revised manuscript, another HCC mouse model has been used to further illustrate whether tyrosine dependency is a common feature of liver tumorigenesis. Mice were injected with the plasmids of myr-AKT and NRASG12V via hydrodynamic tail vein injection to induce HCC tumorigenesis, together with feeding a tyrosine-modified diet (schematic representation provided in the Response Figure 2-5 A). The results demonstrated that tyrosine restriction also significantly attenuated the progression of AKT/NRASG12V-driven HCC (Response Figure 2-5, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S8B-S8D). This further supports the notion that tyrosine dependency represents a common characteristic of liver cancer. A brief description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 9, Lines 224-231).
Furthermore, as raised by the reviewer in this question and question 6, we found that the hepatocellular carcinoma’s dependence on tyrosine was determined by its protein synthesis activity. Specifically, tumor cells exhibiting higher protein synthesis activity show greater inhibition of cell growth upon tyrosine restriction. We measured protein synthesis activity, the expression of MYC, YARS1, and the tyrosine metabolism gene set in seven HCC cell lines and one normal hepatic cell line (THLE-2). The results revealed that the expression levels of MYC in the four tumor cell lines (SNU398, SNU449, PLCPRF5, and HCCLM3) used in our original manuscript were different. Relative to the expression levels of MYC in THLE-2, SNU449 and PLCPRF5 exhibited similar levels, whereas HCCLM3 and SNU398 showed elevated levels. Notably, these four HCC lines demonstrated higher protein synthesis activity and elevated YARS1 expression compared to normal hepatocytes (Response Figure 2-5 D, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S8E). Thus, these four HCC cell lines demonstrated a higher dependence on YARS1 or stronger tyrosine sensitivity, which also explains the reviewer’s comment in question 6, stating that although MYC regulates YARS1 transcription, YARS1 protein levels correlate more strongly with protein synthesis activity. A brief description has also been added to the revised manuscript (Page 9, Line 231 to Page 10, Line 239).
Furthermore, tyrosine restriction was less effective at inhibiting cell proliferation in the cell lines with low protein synthesis activity (THLE-2 or HEPG2), compared to those with high protein synthesis activity (SNU398 or PLCPRF5) (Response Figure 2-5 E, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S8F). Moreover, we found in SNU449 cells with low basal protein synthesis, MYC overexpression increased protein synthesis, thereby potentiating the inhibitory effect of tyrosine restriction (the increased inhibition degree from 37% to 55%), whereas MYC knockdown in SNU398 cells with high protein synthesis activity to reduce protein synthesis activity, decreased this inhibitory effect of tyrosine restriction (the decreased inhibition degree from 63% to 51%) (Response Figure 2-5 F, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S8G). These results indicated that MYC overexpression increased the burden on ribosome translation, rendering the cells more susceptible to tyrosine depletion, which resulted in a greater suppression of cell growth upon tyrosine depletion. A similar phenomenon has also been observed in RNA splicing stage that MYC overexpression increases burden on the core spliceosome in human B-cell line P493-6, thus significantly improving anti-proliferative capacity upon splicing factor BUD31 knockdown (Extended Data Figure 10b) (Hsu et al, 2015) (PMID:26331541). Collectively, these results demonstrate that tyrosine dependency in HCC cells is primarily governed by global protein synthesis activity, rather than being specifically tied to MYC-driven oncogenesis. The brief description (Page 10, Lines 239-248) and discussion (Page 25, Lines 672-674) have also been added to the revised manuscript.

9. ISR Pathway : the authors make no mention to the ISR which is canonically activated in response to AA limitation via GCN2/eif2a/ATF4. This is a key mechanistic gap, especially since uncharged tRNAs are canonical activators of GCN2, several markers observed (e.g. SLC7A5, SLC7A11, oxidative stress response genes) are known ATF4 target genes, and proteins upregulated upon tyrosine deprivation are clustered in hallmarks that are common to amino acid restriction (autophagy, L-amino acid transport etc). The ISR could influence lipid metabolism and ferroptosis, potentially confounding the attribution to SCD1 downregulation. Have the authors assessed ISR activation in response to tyrosine depletion or YARS1 KD? This pathway should be acknowledged.
Response: We genuinely appreciate your insightful comment. As described by the reviewer, GCN2 is a key cellular sensor of amino acid deprivation. When amino acid availability becomes scarce, GCN2 kinase is activated by direct binding to uncharged tRNAs. Then, GCN2 promotes restoration of amino acid levels by up-regulating ATF4 target genes involved in amino acid biosynthesis and transport (Costa-Mattioli & Walter, 2020; Malnassy et al, 2024) (PMID: 32327570, 38768690). We found that there was not associated with any sign of integrated stress response (ISR) after tyrosine deprivation or YARS1 knockdown for 48h in SNU398 cells (Response Figure 2-9 A), which was also observed in threonine restriction in glioblastoma stem cells (Figure 5i) (Wu et al, 2024) (PMID: 38519786) or VARS knockdown in melanoma cells (Extended Data Figure 5b) (El-Hachem et al, 2024) (PMID: 38849541). However, upon prolonging tyrosine restriction or YARS1 knockdown to 72h, a time point used in our original manuscript to detect the change of transcriptomic and proteomic after tyrosine translation limitation, we observed significant activation of the GCN2-eIF2α-ATF4 axis, as shown by increased phosphorylation levels of GCN2 and eIF2α, and elevated protein levels of ATF4, indicating that integrated stress response is activated to respond to tyrosine translation limitation and reestablish physiological homeostasis (Response Figure 2-9 B, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S11E). A brief description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 12, Lines 317-321).
The Integrated Stress Response (ISR) is characterized by the upregulation and activation of ATF4. This response elicits a dichotomous functional outcome: low-level or short-term activation promotes cell survival, whereas prolonged or intense activation drives cell death (Tang et al, 2024) (Wortel et al, 2017) (PMID: 38383612, 28797581). ATF4 directs these opposing cellular fates by regulating a broad set of target genes through complex mechanisms operating at transcriptional, translational, and post-translational levels, and via interactions with other transcription factors. Especially, when considering its involvement in ferroptosis, the ATF4 pathway can either inhibit or promote ferroptosis. Several target genes of ATF4, including HSPA5, SLC7A11, and NUPR1, act as negative regulators of ferroptosis. Conversely, other ATF4 target genes, such as BTG1, DDIT3, CHAC1, and SLC1A5, positively regulate ferroptosis (Tang et al., 2024) (PMID: 38383612). This intricate relationship underscores the complexity of cellular responses to varying stress levels. Thus, although ATF4 serves as a common mediator, the ultimate transcriptional and physiological outcome is determined by the specific cellular context, stress type, and duration of stimulation.
In this study, we found that tyrosine restriction activated the ISR, as evidenced by the upregulation of ATF4 expression (Response Figure 2-9 B, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S11E). Consistent with the model that ATF4 target gene activation depends on stress severity, cellular context, and stimulus duration, our transcriptomic analysis identified a set of genes induced by ATF4 under this condition. Among these, canonical anti-ferroptotic genes such as SLC7A11 and NUPR1 were upregulated, along with several pro-ferroptotic genes, including BTG1, DDIT3 and CHAC1 (Response Figure 2-9 C). This co-activation of antagonistic target genes indicates that the ISR may play a dual role in mediating cellular responses to tyrosine restriction.

(C) Transcriptomics data analysis of ATF4 target gene expression in SNU398 cells cultured in tyrosine-modified mediums (n = 3).
10. Fatty acid metabolism and link to ferroptosis: fatty acid composition is known to change under metabolic stress or ISR activation. Can the authors uncouple the effects of tyrosine depletion on MUFA/PUFA balance from its protenogenic role in SCD1 synthesis? Would MUFA supplementation rescue ferroptosis induced by tyrosine depletion, MYC KD, or YARS1 KD? Does SCD1 KD alone recapitulate the lipid peroxidation phenotypes?
Response: Thanks for your professional advice. As a rate-limiting enzyme for monounsaturated fatty acid (MUFA) biosynthesis, SCD1 reduction or inhibition promotes a shift from MUFAs to PUFAs in cellular lipid composition and induces ferroptosis (Bogie et al, 2020; Ding et al, 2023; Glowacka et al, 2024; Schwab et al, 2024; Thurmer et al, 2022; Zhao et al, 2022) (PMID: 32097464, 37805657, 39572570, 39009641, 35624087, 36197994). In high-ZEB1-expressing cancer cells, ZEB1 knockdown represses the expression of enzymes important for MUFA biosynthesis (including SCD1 and FASN), thereby significantly altering the ratio of PUFA/MUFA and inducing ferroptosis (Figure 2c) (Schwab et al., 2024) (PMID: 39009641). In FaDu cancer cells, SCD1 inhibition causes a 3-fold reduction in MUFA levels, and the PUFA/MUFA ratio increases substantially more in the presence of SCD1 inhibitors (Figure 5h-5j) (Glowacka et al., 2024) (PMID: 39572570). Thus, in our original manuscript, we proposed that tyrosine restriction suppressed SCD1 translation in a codon-dependent manner, leading to an imbalance in MUFA/PUFA. Furthermore, as noted by the reviewers, the impact of tyrosine deprivation on the MUFA/PUFA balance may also be mediated through the activation of ISR. Previous study has found that ISR activation significantly alters cellular lipid composition, particularly leading to significant accumulation of PUFAs containing at least three double bonds (20:4, 22:4, 22:5, 24:6) (Supplementary Fig.7f, 7g) (Labbe et al, 2024) (PMID: 39333061). Thus, based on the results from response Figure 2-9 B, i.e., induced ISR activation upon tyrosine deprivation, we propose that the altered intracellular MUFA/PUFA balance may be attributed to a dual mechanism: (i) tyrosine-mediated translation regulation of SCD1, and (ii) ISR activation-driven remodeling of lipid composition under tyrosine restriction. The brief description has also been added to the revised manuscript (Page 13, Lines 334-336).
SCD1 catalyzes the desaturation of saturated fatty acids, principally stearic acid (18:0) and palmitic acid (16:0), to their Δ9-monounsaturated counterparts, oleic acid (18:1) and palmitoleic acid (16:1) (Thurmer et al., 2022) (PMID: 35624087). Previous studies have found that ferroptosis induced by MUFA deficiency due to SCD1 knockdown can be rescued by MUFA supplementation (Sokol et al, 2025; Zhao et al., 2022) (PMID: 39442523, 36197994). Similarly, we demonstrated that supplementation with oleic acid and palmitoleic acid (hereafter referred to as MUFA) effectively alleviated ferroptosis triggered by tyrosine restriction, YARS1 knockdown, or MYC knockdown, as evidenced by decreased lipid peroxidation levels (Response Figure 2-10 A-C, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S19K-S19M). Furthermore, SCD1 knockdown resulted in increased lipid peroxidation (Response Figure 2-10 D, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S19N). Thus, these findings suggest that restricting tyrosine availability induces ferroptosis by disrupting the MUFA/PUFA balance, whereas MUFA supplementation significantly alleviates it. The brief description has also been added to the revised manuscript (Page 19, Lines 505-509).

15. Figure 2B/2C, Lines 126-128: The enrichment of tyrosine codons in translationally upregulated proteins may reflect general increases in protein synthesis. Would this not also be true for other amino acids? Is this increased utilization of tyrosine for protein synthesis tyrosine-specific or a global phenomenon associated with tumour progression?
Response: Thanks for this important question. As highlighted by the reviewer, in our original manuscript, we demonstrated that both tyrosine uptake and its incorporation ratio into proteins are significantly higher in HCC tissues compared to normal liver tissues by using an ex vivo isotopic tracer method (Figure 2B and 2C in the current revised manuscript). To investigate whether this is attributed to increased protein synthesis in tumors, we performed an in-depth analysis of amino acid and codon enrichment in proteins with translation upregulated and downregulated in HCC patients (Response 2-14 A, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure 2H). This analysis revealed that the enrichment levels of only a subset of amino acids and their corresponding cognate codons were elevated (e.g., lysine and tyrosine) within HCC tissue, while others were reduced (e.g., alanine). This indicates that although protein synthesis generally increases during HCC progression, the utilization of some, but not all, amino acids increase; in some cases, it even decreases. This phenomenon has also been observed in melanoma, leukemia, and breast cancer. Specifically, the translational utilization of valine is notably increased in melanoma and leukemia, thereby facilitating mitochondrial oxidative respiration and fatty acid oxidation (El-Hachem et al., 2024; Thandapani et al, 2022) (PMID: 38849541, 34937946). In contrast, in breast cancer, translational utilization of leucine is significantly suppressed, thereby inhibiting the translation of growth-suppressive genes (Passarelli et al, 2022) (PMID: 35288656). These findings suggest that during tumor progression, there is an increased translational utilization of specific amino acids to enhance protein synthesis.
Moreover, to further identify that the increased translational utilization of tyrosine is a specific feature of liver tumor progression, we compared the uptake differences of tyrosine, lysine, and alanine between tumor tissues and normal tissues. The results showed that while the uptake rates of both tyrosine and lysine were significantly elevated in tumor tissues compared to normal tissues (Response Figure 2-14 B up, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S6G), only tyrosine exhibited a significantly higher incorporation ratio into protein synthesis within HCC (Response Figure 2-14 B bottom, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S6G). We found that YARS1 and its cognate isoacceptor tRNA-TyrGUA were significantly upregulated in tumors. In contrast, KARS1 (lysine-tRNA ligase) and AARS1 (alanine-tRNA synthetase), responsible for charging lysine and alanine, respectively, were markedly downregulated in tumor tissues compared to normal tissues (Response Figure 2-10 C, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S6H). Correspondingly, the levels of tRNA-LysCUU showed a significant decrease, and the levels of tRNA-Ala remained unchanged. These results suggest that enhanced amino acid uptake, coupled with elevated levels of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and their cognate tRNAs, is essential for supporting the increased translational utilization of amino acids in tumors (Response Figure 2-10 D, corresponding to the revised manuscript Figure S6I). Collectively, these results demonstrate that the increased consumption of tyrosine for protein synthesis is a key metabolic vulnerability driving liver cancer progression. A brief description has been added to the revised manuscript (Page 8, Lines 177-189).
